These airports were selected to represent diverse geographies, fuel volumes, and facility types. This report refers to both jet fuel and Jet A. Jet fuel is a broader term that includes both Jet A and other types of jet fuel used by the military, because there are terminals in New England solely providing jet fuel to the military. Jet A is used by commercial and general aviation aircraft and is blended with SAF for use in the same aircraft. At the time this study was prepared, the military is using Jet A for commercial-type aircraft in its fleet but does not use SAF blends currently. 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. The United States both imports and exports Jet A, driven by the location of refineries and availability of infrastructure to move fuels by multiple modes. New England receives a significant portion of their Jet A supply from Canada due to proximity of a large refinery. In 2024, the United States consumed 26 billion gallons of Jet A, representing approximately 26% of world consumption. Unlike gasoline and diesel, Jet A consumption continues to increase, illustrating the need for solutions to reduce emission impacts from aircraft (EIA 2025f). Based on 2023 U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) data, New England Jet A consumption represented roughly 3% of national consumption (Table 2, EIA 2025d). BOS consumes more fuel than all other New England airports combined (Table 3, EIA 2025d).
